draft.answer: Yes, but not as separate git repos, and not by moving directories yet. All three judges picked the same plan. Keep one repository and first draw about 12 named pieces over the existing folders. A committed manifest and a ratchet gate in CI enforce them, so no file moves and no roadmap ownershipPaths string changes; this can start today. The frightening "64-area cycle" comes from rolling files up into areas. At file level there are only 6 runtime cycles covering 40 files, and the proven minimum for the proposed layering is 94 runtime import statements. Once a lower piece is proven clean (construction, printing, the rules engine plus simulation), it becomes an npm-workspace package under packages/ that the app consumes as TypeScript source, and the battlemech unit catalog becomes a pinned, fetched data artifact. The campaign, multiplayer and events core stays in the app until the roadmap program lets go of those paths. Separate repos would make roughly 3 of every 4 rules-engine changes a publish-then-bump chain, and no version of the split shortens the 3-5 minute pre-commit build on its own.
draft.recommendedShape:
One repo, layered in place first and packaged later ("boundaries-in-place", grafted with the workspaces extraction mechanics).

(1) A committed piece manifest assigns every src path to one of about 12 pieces, in this layer order: foundation, then persistence-infra, then construction, then printing and tactical (siblings), then events, then kernel, then campaign, then p2p, then multiplayer, then the app layers (services, stores, ui and api). Desktop and the battlemech catalog sit outside the layers.

(2) A TypeScript-parser ratchet gate reads the manifest. It lives at scripts/boundaries/validate-module-boundaries.mjs, a path no ledger entry owns. It fails on any new upward or forbidden-sibling import, or any new import of a non-entry file, and it requires the baseline to shrink. Two oxlint rules back it up: import/no-cycle with ignoreTypes, and per-piece no-restricted-imports using regex patterns. Each rule is switched to error only once its count reaches 0. Per-piece `tsc` composite probes prove that each piece's type closure stays inside the pieces it is allowed to import.

(3) A piece graduates to a private npm-workspace package when four things hold: 0 gate violations, a green probe, no non-terminal roadmap owner, and a consumer reason. The package is consumed as TS source (packages/*, `transpilePackages`, no build, no publish). The Next app stays at the repo root. desktop/ stays its own non-workspace package on npm, not pnpm. Every package gets three-part enforcement: an oxlint ban on `@/`, a tsconfig with no `paths`, and a resolved-import boundary test. A transitional `@/` alias keeps planned lane branches mergeable.

(4) The battlemech catalog (public/data/units/battlemechs) leaves the tree as a pinned artifact, following the existing config/mm-data-assets.json and scripts/mm-data/fetch-assets.ts pattern.

(5) Separate repos stay a later option. The trigger is a re-run of the co-change measurement showing a package's commits rarely touch the app, well below today's 74% for the rules code.

phases.name: Phase 0: build-time quick win (owner decision; independent of any split)

Drop one of the two, or move the full build to CI, and use `jest --changedSince` for affected tests. This cuts time on every TS commit, and no package split does. It interacts with the repo's verify-before-claiming rules, so it needs the owner's call.

scores.rationale: This design has the best cost-to-gain ratio for a solo maintainer who pays for every cross-repo change. I independently re-verified its central claim with judge1-scc.js over file-edges.json. The file-level runtime graph has exactly 6 cycles covering 40 files: utils/gameplay 20+3, components/customizer 9, stores/useGameplayStore 3, lib/campaign/sync 3 and lib/multiplayer/server 2. Counting type-only imports, there are 27 cycles over 258 files, the largest 124 and 65. So the 64-area SCC comes from rolling files up into areas, and a file-level ratchet gate is tractable. The plan moves no directories and changes no ownershipPaths strings. The new files go in unowned paths: I checked that docs/qc and scripts/boundaries have no owners. It uses tools that are already installed (oxlint 1.43.0, TypeScript). Undoing it means deleting a gate script and a manifest. Weaknesses: 1) It does not speed up the build. The .husky/pre-commit:13-18 full next build and the lint-staged tsc both stay. 2) It adds friction to roadmap units that touch lib/campaign. 3) Its roadmap-ownership statement for phase B is wrong (see the errors list). 4) Most of the real untangling is in campaign (66 of 104 runtime violations), which stays deferred.

This is the right destination for the lower layers, and the best-engineered extraction plan. It puts package-enforced direction on 42% of production files. It has named ports for Toast, matchLogStorage, ReplaySurfaceGate and FormulaStore. I confirmed matchLogStorage at InteractiveSession.ts:21,292,772 and sessionEvents.ts:6, and Toast at persistence.ts:1. It uses a transitional alias so moves don't conflict with every lane worktree. It correctly keeps the app at the repo root (next.config.ts:111-115 confirmed) and keeps desktop out of the workspace. The tsx probe finding matters: '@/' resolves back into the app from inside a package, so exports alone enforce nothing. Costs: about 12,000 specifier rewrites, 156 jest.mock targets and 853 source-ref literals. Scaffolding has to be proven for standalone hydrate, Docker and Electron; I confirmed hydrate copies only src and tsconfig. It rewrites 16 ownership refs, including evidence strings on complete and main-verified nodes, and container refs silently stop covering moved code. It gives no pre-commit speed-up. Its steps 0-2 are essentially the boundaries-in-place design, so as an overall plan it is dominated by doing that design first.

The analysis is honest and well measured: exact minimum back-edge search, 90-day co-change, and ownership breakage per partition. It correctly rejects the full split, which had 29.8% cross-repo commits and broke 18 non-complete units. But even the narrow split E would have turned 42 of 57 rules commits (74%) into a publish-then-bump chain. For one maintainer with agents, that is an ongoing tax on most rules changes. It also adds registry credentials to every install path; I confirmed there is no tracked .npmrc today. Specs would stop landing atomically with code (26 of 57 rules commits touched openspec). Undoing a filter-repo extraction is expensive. Its possible speed gain, a smaller app type-check program, is marked unverified. Its own recommendation is to rehearse in-repo first and extract only if co-change falls. That concedes the workspace path, so as a design it is a later, conditional option, not a plan.

scores.rationale: Seen from build and CI, this design does no harm now and keeps later options open. It moves no paths, so validate-roadmap's existsSync checks at :264-265 and :367-369 are untouched. At HEAD units.json has 80 units (complete 34, planned 41, blocked 4, main-verified 1) and none are in IN_FLIGHT_STATES (validate-roadmap.mjs:59), which I re-checked. The CI cost is small and I verified it: oxlint import/no-cycle with ignoreTypes reports exactly 40 problems (oxlint-nocycle-runtime.txt); the repo lint shows 84 problems, all warnings (oxlint-repo.txt); the construction tsc probe gives exactly 255 TS6307 errors (tsc-probe/construction.out). The TS-parser gate takes about 6s as a job under the existing required 'Lint and Test' check. It also correctly reframes the 64-area SCC as an effect of grouping files into areas: there are only 6 file-level runtime cycles, covering 40 files. The ratchet design is justified because oxlint has no baseline or suppression flag: `oxlint --help` shows none; the only matching option is -A/--allow. The weakness is speed. The duplicated whole-project type-check stays: lint-staged runs `bash -c 'npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck'` (package.json:336), and next build type-checks the same program because next.config.ts has no ignoreBuildErrors. The full build in .husky/pre-commit, which its own comment puts at about 5 min, also stays. The design admits both costs but leaves out the cheap fix: the hook can be path-aware without packages. It also adds friction to the loop, because roadmap units must edit the baseline explicitly. That friction is visible and deliberate.

This is the most rigorous design for actually creating packages, and its build and CI facts check out. The Dockerfile copies only the root package.json and package-lock.json before `npm ci` (lines 15-16, 18 and 31-32; stage 1 also runs `--ignore-scripts` then `npm rebuild better-sqlite3`). server.js:449-463 loads six multiplayer .ts modules plus SQLiteService through tsx/cjs. next.config.ts:115 sets outputFileTracingRoot to process.cwd(). Root tsconfig include ['**/*.ts'] (line 27) does cover packages/. Its junction probe shows tsx 4.22.4 resolves `@/` from inside a linked package, which closes the tooling lane's UNVERIFIED item and correctly makes the lint ban, the no-paths tsconfig and the boundary test all mandatory. Its handling of native modules is sound: npm rather than pnpm, desktop stays outside the workspace, and better-sqlite3 stays in the app so no package wraps it. On speed it is candid and correct. Packages consumed as TypeScript source are compiled inside next build, so the pre-commit build does not get faster. Each package's no-paths tsconfig adds another tsc pass on top of today's two type-checks, which is a net loss locally unless it runs only in CI. Migration risk is high: about 12,000 specifier rewrites, 156 jest.mock targets and 853 'src/...' literals, each PR passing a roughly 5-minute hook. Step 3 must also re-verify standalone hydrate, Docker and Electron on three OSes. Reversibility is medium: the transitional aliases help, but after the alias codemod, moving back is another large rewrite.

The measurements are honest, and the design argues itself down to partition E. On build speed it is the only design that could shrink the app's type-check and next build program: the compiled rules package ships .d.ts for 2,551 files. That gain is labelled INFERENCE and was never probed. Against it: every rules change pays publish-then-bump (42 of 57 rules commits, 74%, also touched app source); registry auth becomes a dependency of CI, the Dockerfile's `npm ci`, the Electron better-sqlite3 rebuild and every agent worktree (no .npmrc is tracked, which I confirmed); and the rules repo needs its own duplicated jest, oxlint, husky and CI plus a downstream canary. Its own step 3 is simply the workspaces design, so it only adds value after that design succeeds. Taking the extra step to a separate repo is hard to undo: filter-repo history, a published version line, and specs split across repos. The catalog-data satellite, by contrast, is low-risk and a clear build and CI win: 21 MB and 4,226 JSON files leave the tree, and the existing mm-data fetch pattern (config/mm-data-assets.json) can be reused.

Nothing moves, so the existsSync and unit-within-node checks keep passing. I confirmed its evidence exists in scratch: the oxlint no-cycle run reports 40 findings, the construction tsc probe gives exactly 255 TS6307 errors, the kernel3 probe output is empty, and `git diff f6e3599a3 31d01f4ab -- src` is empty. The loop does pay a real cost. Once the ratchet gate blocks on regression, 19 non-terminal units that own paths under src (U19, U35, U58, U21, U36, U37, U38, U23, U43, U24, U44, U45, U26, U46-U50, U56) must either add no new upward import or edit the baseline in their PR. That is extra review load, but it is visible and reversible. Maintainability: it enforces the direction of imports and gives a numbered worklist, but it cannot yet fix the campaign/multiplayer core, which is 66 of the 104 runtime violations and sits in roadmap-owned code. Speed: no gain; the 3-5 minute pre-commit build is unchanged and the gate adds about 6 s. Reversibility: it is a manifest, a script and lint config, so it can be deleted in one PR.

Steps 0-2 are the same zero-move work as boundaries-in-place. The package moves in steps 3-7 do touch the ledger. I re-measured the refs: foundation 7 (src/types/multiplayer on R2.combat, U4 and U45; src/types/campaign on R7.versions, R7.provenance and R8.opportunities; UnitCombatState.ts on R9.roster-damage), construction 6, rules 3 (src/engine on R2.combat; src/utils/gameplay/gameState on R2.multiplayer-client and U37). Several of these belong to complete or main-verified nodes, so historical evidence strings would have to be edited. Its most valuable finding for the loop is correct and the other designs miss it. The parent refs stay valid while silently losing coverage: 10 nodes own the exact string `src`, and U45 owns `src/lib`. The --next scheduler (:541-560) uses pathsOverlap on strings, so a unit owning src/... would not collide with work under packages/construction. That makes the overlap scheduler quietly unsound after the moves. The design also usefully measured that tsx resolves `@/` from inside a junction-linked package, so exports alone enforce nothing. The transitional alias keeps planned branches mergeable. Migration risk is moderate: standalone hydrate, Docker, Electron and 3-OS verification, and about 12,000 specifiers. Speed does not improve without affected-only tooling. Reversal means moving directories back and rewriting the ledger strings again.

The validator works against a single repoRoot. existsSync at :264-265 and :367-368 and the in-repo overlap scheduler cannot follow paths into another repo without a redesign ('repo:path' syntax), and the design admits this. Even the narrow partition E moves paths owned by R2.combat (src/engine), R7.versions (src/services/units), R9.equipment-loader (3 files), R9.validation-order (2 files), R2.multiplayer-client and U37 (src/utils/gameplay/gameState). The same silent coverage loss applies under the 10 exact `src` owners. Its own co-change number argues against it: 42 of 57 rules commits in 90 days (74%) also touched app production source, so most roadmap units that touch rules would become publish-then-bump chains across two PRs and two repos, which the unit/PR/OWNER-RULING ledger cannot express. Registry credentials would be needed on every agent worktree, and no .npmrc is tracked today. The full split A hits 39 of 75 nodes and 18+ non-terminal units. It may speed up the app's type check (2,551 files replaced by .d.ts, unverified), but publish cycles slow the loop. Reversing a filter-repo extraction is expensive. The measurement work (exact minimum back-edge set, co-change gate) is its best contribution.
